text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

महोदय,

सविनय निवेदन है कि मैं, निशु आज़ाद, सोशल मीडिया प्लेटफॉर्म X की उपयोगकर्ता हूँ। मेरे X अकाउंट को सस्पेंड किए जाने के संबंध में मेरे मन में यह आशंका उत्पन्न हुई है कि कहीं इस कार्रवाई के पीछे मेरे प्रति किसी प्रकार का जातिगत भेदभाव तो नहीं है।

यदि मेरे अकाउंट पर की गई कार्रवाई में जाति के आधार पर भेदभाव हुआ है, तो यह एक गंभीर विषय है, जिसकी निष्पक्ष जाँच की जानी चाहिए। मैं संबंधित प्लेटफॉर्म से यह जानना चाहती हूँ कि मेरा अकाउंट किन विशिष्ट नियमों के उल्लंघन के कारण सस्पेंड किया गया और क्या इसी प्रकार के मामलों में सभी उपयोगकर्ताओं के साथ समान नीति अपनाई जाती है।

FEDAI’s circular dated 21 August 2026 (SPL-05/Trade/2026) clarifies foreign exchange billing and remittance practices for freight forwarders, with important takeaways for businesses and authorised dealer banks.

Here are the key highlights:

🔹 Foreign currency collections must have an underlying liability
An Indian resident receiving foreign exchange as a pass-through intermediary should collect it towards an underlying foreign exchange liability, for onward remittance to a person resident outside India.

🔹 No exchange margin or mark-up by the pass-through intermediary
The intermediary cannot quote an exchange rate or collect an exchange margin/mark-up on such transactions. The foreign currency collected should reflect the amount required to meet the overseas liability.

🔹 Foreign currency remittances within India must not exceed the overseas invoice
For freight-forwarding transactions, the amount should not exceed the invoice raised by the overseas transporter. Banks should verify the underlying transaction and supporting documents to establish the actual foreign exchange liability.

🔹 Intermediary service charges should be denominated in INR
Charges for the Indian intermediary’s services should be denominated in INR where those charges are not being remitted to a person resident outside India.

🔹 Industry circulars require verification
Before relying on an industry circular or advisory, banks should verify its authenticity, current validity and applicability to the transaction.

The key takeaway: distinguish the overseas foreign exchange liability from the Indian intermediary’s own service charges, and support the transaction with clear documentation.

For banking and logistics professionals, these clarifications underline the importance of transparent billing and transaction-level due diligence.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

How I ($1MM/year seller) find winning Amazon FBA products in 2026

Quick context: ~9 years selling on Amazon, 3 brands, ~1,500 SKUs (mostly toys & games), 3 VAs, $1MM/year at ~40% margin. Numbers verified by https://t.co/HnGPqhlwMu and the mods of r/FulfillmentByAmazon: https://t.co/e14qmNmwm5

Below is the process my team and I use to find products. I've broken down a bunch of Amazon stores over the last few months, and the same process keeps working for me, so here it is. No tool needed to start, just Amazon and a spreadsheet.

STEP 1 - Start from stores that already win, not from keywords or individual products

• Keyword tools tell you what people search for. They don't tell you who makes money.
• Individual products also don't tell the whole story - I have 1,500 SKUs, most of them don't make much money, but combined they made me a business.
• Find brands that started recently (6-12 months) and already sell well - that proves the niche is still open to new entrants
• Amazon's own "X+ bought in past month" on each listing, summed across their ASINs, gives you a revenue estimate that's surprisingly close

STEP 2 - Ask ONE question: where did the founder add value ?

• Almost everything on Amazon is made by the same Chinese factories. If the only thing you add is a logo, you're competing on price - and that's a race to zero margin
• The products I keep seeing with HIGH margins are ones where the customer pays for something made once and sold many times: a DESIGN (puzzles, card games, kitchen gadgets with a cute/creative shape), or a product paired with an app/course
• People buy a puzzle for the picture, not the cardboard. That's why a $3 puzzle sells for $20 - same goes for card games, posters, or anything like that
• This is my framework from running my own brand, not something I can prove - but the stores I analyse fit it a lot
• I stay away from food and supplements - no experience there, so I won't pretend to advise on them (but they do essentially follow the same pattern - create a good recipe once and sell the food many times)

STEP 3 - Work out the real margin (this kills 80% of ideas)

Per-unit economics for the store you're looking at:

• Revenue = "bought in past month" x price, for every ASIN
• COGS = ask 3-5 suppliers on Alibaba for a quote on the same product at 100 MOQ. Real quotes, not guesses
• FBA fees + 15% referral fee - Amazon's revenue calculator does this
• PPC = CPC x monthly search volume x estimated CTR, for the keywords they bid on
• What's left is profit. I mostly ignore anything that ends up under ~25% margin

STEP 4 - Check how they get their sales

• Almost no PPC and still selling? The product itself converts. Great sign.
• Bringing traffic from outside of Amazon ? You'll have to understand if you can replicate their methods
• Sales spread across many SKUs, or one hero SKU ? One hero SKU = you have to win one fight. Many SKUs = they have a design pipeline you'd have to match

STEP 5 - Price the validation, not the dream

• Estimate how much it would cost you to test each brand you're thinking of launching. At the end of the day, in order to succeed, you'll need multiple tries (nobody has a 100% success rate). You want to try as many businesses as possible, as quickly as possible, for as cheap as possible.
• Cost to test = MOQ (e.g. 100 units x $5.40 = $540) + shipping + ONE month of ads on a few long tail keywords
• Some products you might be able to POD (print on demand) - that is, only *produce* the product AFTER you get the order. This is NOT dropshipping. You might even have to do it at a loss per order. This is just to validate demand. If you see there is demand for your product - shut off the listing and go produce it in China.
• If you can't test it for well under your budget, it's not a validation, it's a bet

WHY AM I GIVING THIS AWAY ?

• Fair question - I'd ask it too
• I used to think I should keep the good niches "secret". I don't anymore - people who know how to research will find them either way, and there's still a LOT of work and risk to take before any niche pays you.
• There's a huge amount of good niches to get into, but an even huger amount of niches that will DEFINITELY lose you money.
• I see Amazon newbies making the most basic mistakes all the time - because they don't understand that they gotta ADD VALUE to make money.

This video is said to be from 2009. Look at how the Election Commission of India functioned then, and compare it with what is happening today.

The Election Commission freely encouraged citizens to exercise their voting rights. Its advertisements highlighted the problems people faced in everyday life, including corruption, poor education, inadequate healthcare, crumbling infrastructure and bad governance, and reminded them that the power to change these conditions lay in their votes.

The central purpose was to promote universal adult franchise, encourage electoral participation and increase voter turnout.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

In April of 2025, eMudhra (an Indian Certificate Authority), published 8 intermediate CA keys which were so weak that a small child could guess the numbers in a few seconds.

One of the private keys was, literally, 4.

Just… 4.

This massive problem was not made public until October 17th of this year, when it was discovered by an anonymous guy on the Internet who goes only by “Wayne” (like “Cher”…. but… “Wayne”).

What this means in practical terms: It has been trivially simple, for the last year and a half, to create fake “secure” HTTPS certificates.  (One person even created a fake HTTPS certificate for a https://t.co/9rSoW8koVR subdomain.)

It took Mozilla 3 days, after learning about this (from “Wayne”), before they updated their certificate list (which many open source projects — including curl and Python — rely upon).

As of this moment, many systems are still vulnerable (including macOS).

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia 

#Samsung #SamsungIndia #GalaxyS25Ultra #SamsungService #Nagpur #ConsumerRights #scamservice

My Mother
“When I was pregnant with you I was under pressure to have an abortion but I refused. I chose instead to bring you into this world.”
My mother did not hesitate to bring up the circumstances around my birth and conception every time I tried her patience as a young boy. Granted, she always told me she loved me, but I got to know my chequered history quite early. 
“Your father’s parents owned a shop and the women who worked there assured me that it was unacceptable and totally reprehensible, a taboo, for an African woman and an Asian man to get together, let alone produce a child from that union. The only solution they said, was to perform an abortion and end that life before it even began. But I refused!"
I was conceived towards the end of the 60s, a few years into Uganda’s journey as an independent country, a few years before Idi Amin Dada started his rule in Uganda. I am told it was the time of miniskirts and twist dancing in Uganda, and the time of the American sex revolution!
My father was a young Asian of (most likely) Indian descent whose family was one of the trading families in Masaka. He was a student at Makerere University, and that is the extent of my knowledge about my father. 
Soon after I was born, President Iddi Amin declared an economic war of indigenization and my father was among those who were deported/expelled out of Uganda. The History of Uganda is such that Asians, particularly Indians took the lion’s share of trading licences. President Amin wanted to reverse this unfair advantage but unfortunately, it meant I would never get to meet my father or his family. Not only was I born in a conflicted relationship of races, I never got a chance to know who my father was, nor his family. Despite the great love and acceptance that I received from my mother, siblings and my Baganda tribal family, I always felt a great sense of “father hunger” - that yearning for fatherly protection, provision and affirmation which only a Dad could provide.
My mother was a primary school teacher who was struggling to raise eight children as a single parent. She had been married to James Kyeyune, a medical officer and they were blessed with six children but their marriage broke down. My mother always told me that she could not accept being a co-wife. My step father had brought another wife home and she could not accept the idea of sharing a husband. Despite the efforts of the good catholic bishops who intervened to smooth things over, the marriage broke down and she moved away in the mid-60s to start a new life as a teacher and a single mother.
I was born into a family of seven other children, five boys and two girls. Dickson, the eldest had gone off to join the police force, Joseph the second born and Edward the fifth born stayed with their paternal grandparents. Clare and Fred were students in a Catholic boarding school and came home only during the holidays. This meant that the three youngest children Florence, John and myself were the ones who stayed home with mother.
Owing to my bi-racial parentage, my looks were quite different from the rest of the family and the children around me. I had big curly hair unlike my brother’s kinky hair. I had much lighter skin due to my father’s suspected Asian descent.
In our Baganda culture, the name of a child is based on the clan of the father and in the absence of my biological father, my mother gave me the names of her father, Ssempa which meant that I belonged to my mother’s clan; symbolically represented by the colobus monkey (Nkima). My grandfather, Alipo Ssempa was an educated British colonial government administrator and interpreter in Masaka. Sadly, I never got to meet him as death took him before we could meet. His father, Bisakka or Bishaka who was my great grandfather had been a noteworthy regional trader in the Buganda, Ankole, Bunyoro, Rwanda and Tanzania region. He was called Bisaka, a name very closely related to Kisaka which is a large cluster or collection of trees and bushes which occurs on the savannah plains and hills in this region. It’s like an individual collection of a family of trees and bushes which are separated from others by savannah grass fields. Just as his name implies, my great grandfather had eighty households which made up his large family!
Bisaka was known as Bishaka by the western Ankole-Rwanda tribes whose language is characterized by the ‘sh’ making him multi tribal/multi lingual and multi-wifey. Unfortunately, this great trader and lover of the sweet affections of the beautiful women of Buganda, Ankole, Rwanda and Tanzania region suffered an early death which led to the scattering of the whole family. My great grandmother Venecka Munaku Atambuza mwoyo [the poor walks guided by the spirit] and her sister who had also been a co-wife branched out Eastward and settled between Mityebiri/ Minziro in Rakai and Buyikuzi in Lukaya which is half way between Kampala city and Masaka town. Thus I carried the genes of Bisaka and the name of his son Ssempa, a fact which made people do a double take every time they met the bi-racial child with a native African name. It was not the norm.
These bio-genetical differences were much more pronounced in my childhood. I stuck out both in the classroom and on the children’s playfield. I can compare it to being the only black student in an all-white students school or being the only white student at an all-black-African students school. To some, I was an object of curiosity and I often had to bear the discomfort of having my hair felt, so the kids with kinky hair could feel my curly hair. Most of them were kind, but others would mock me with unkind words,
”Ssempa was forgotten at the airport, the Indians forgot him with the suitcases and boxes at the airport.”
They would laugh and others gave me the monicker, ‘Magoba ga Uganda’ a Luganda phrase meaning “Ugandan profit” which they would explain with youthful logic;
“In the interaction between Uganda and India, Ssempa was the Ugandan profit.”
 These were painful words casually thrown around by some misguided youngsters. They did not reflect the sentiment of the whole Buganda community which accepted me as a son. But in the places where children interacted with minimal adult supervision; the classrooms, playing fields where adults were absent to guide, I was often called painful names, like ‘illegitimate,’ ‘bastard,’ ‘magoba ga Uganda.’ It is a fact of life that some children will mock those who are different or handicapped, maybe they have unusually large ears or nose. This is the foolishness of childhood which fortunately disappears as we grow older. 
Narozali is found in Buyange Parish, Kyanamukakaaka subcounty in Masaka district in the South West of Uganda. It was a large Roman catholic parish with a church, schools and many other projects run by the church. It was located about one hour from Masaka town, on the undulating hills surrounding the shores of Lake Victoria. My mother was a grade one (primary one) teacher at the parish and we stayed in a house provided by the school. My mother was a devout catholic and we attended daily morning mass as well as family evening prayers. We prayed much when there was trouble such as when there was war in the period of 1971-72.
In 1971, the president of Uganda, Apollo Milton Obote was overthrown by his star general, Idid Amin Dada in a military takeover that changed Uganda’s political and economic terrain in which I was to grow up. 

First, the expulsion of Asians in his economic war policy of indigenization was a strange mixture of tragedy and triumph. It was tragic to the Indians whose families had built and run the back bone of the Ugandan economy and were unceremoniously expelled from the country. Most of all the industries, commercial farms, large and small trading shops were owned and run by Indian families who had the technical skills, experience and passion to operate them effectively. They were forced to vacate all of this in a short time not knowing where they were to go. The sudden loss of homes and wealth which had been accumulated for nearly a century led some unfortunate souls to suicides by the river Nile. Others travelled to Canada, England, Kenya and United States where they started a new life. Some ended up succeeding incredibly in their new homes, becoming the economic entrepreneurs of their new homelands.
Soon after Idi Amin became president of Uganda, there was an ill-fated attempt to attack and militarily overthrow him by rebels based out of Tanzania. Our home of Narozali is in the South West region of Uganda’s territory next to Tanzania and at times, it seemed that we were living in a war zone. Military vehicles, jeeps and noisy Israeli-made warplanes above made it difficult to ignore the ongoing conflict. We spent a lot of time praying to God to intervene and even added special supplications to the Virgin Mary who had a special altar with her monument encased in a specially made grotto. Here we earnestly recited the rosary and asked for divine intervention. Providentially, the war ended soon as the attackers were defeated in a bloody massacre! The early efforts by the coalition of anti-Idi Amini forces to remove him militarily were unsuccessful and suffered huge casualties.

For the natives, it was also a mixture of triumph and tragedy. Their struggle for independence from colonial masters had given them political gains without economic gains. The economy was controlled by the Indian merchant families giving little or no space for the emergence of African owned enterprises. This all changed suddenly as Iddi Amin began to apportion out enterprises to the natives. My mother applied to operate a stone quarry but was denied for some reason. However, native Ugandan's got to own and operate all sorts of businesses from industries to merchant shops. While it is true that many ended up being mismanaged and run into the ground, there were others which succeeded.

The expulsion of the Asians/ Indians created a leadership vacuum which forced many Ugandans to quickly learn to trade in various enterprises, giving rise to Ugandan owned business. As a child of dual Asian-Ugandan ancestry, it was a loss for my father’s people, and a gain for my mother’s people. As Nyinamwiru, the daughter of Bukuku lamented when she learnt that her father had been killed by her son Karabumbi Nduhura who was now the new king, 
“My ears cause me to hear both evil and good, for is it not my son who has killed Bukuku? My father is dead, but my son reigns, thus I have sorrow on one arm but joy on the other.” 
This historical account of our ancestors’ dilemma describes my conflicted view of Idi Amin’s expulsion of Indians from Uganda. This view was later to be articulated in my college days by a professor of Political Science at Makerere University who said that Amin’s expulsion of Indians was the single most significant event in economic empowerment of the Ugandan natives. It was quite interesting because, Professor Mahmood Mamdani, was a Ugandan with Asian ancestry, just like me. To date, Uganda, unlike its East African counterparts Kenya and Tanzania has the greatest number of Africans who own business while the other two have businesses still largely owned by the original Asian families who had no Iddi Amin to shake them up.

Excerpts from "Magoba Ga Uganda" the Auto Biography of Pastor Martin Ssempa..Coming out later in July 2024.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

text:
I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). Statement : SBI has told the stock exchanges about its data breach, but not the customers whose data was leaked

New Delhi, 21 October 2026

Today, the State Bank of India told the BSE and the National Stock Exchange, in a disclosure under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, that it has experienced an incident involving the loss of customer data. On 16 October 2026 the bank received alerts from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In that its customers’ data was available on the dark web. Its preliminary analysis of about 3.75 lakh records found 3,897 customer records containing personal information. These include registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs and details linked to loan records. The bank says it does not yet know where the data came from, and it has engaged a CERT-In empanelled agency to find out.

SBI did not detect this breach itself and learnt of it from outside agencies after the data had already been published. On the same day, a threat monitoring account on X flagged a claim by a group calling itself “Siriusim” that it had released 3.75 lakh rows of SBI data and 2,722 PDF documents, including loan applications and account opening forms. The bank’s disclosure does not mention these documents. It also does not say what the remaining records, beyond the 3,897 it has identified, contain.

At the time of this statement, SBI has not said that it has informed any of the affected customers, and its disclosure is silent on the point. Five days passed between the alert and today’s filing. The filing assures investors that the incident has no material impact on the bank’s operations, financial performance or business continuity. However, it does not state anything to the 3,897 people whose phone numbers, dates of birth and home addresses are now with fraudsters. These customers are the most likely to receive calls from persons posing as SBI officials who can recite their account details back to them. A customer cannot guard against a fraud she has not been warned of.

The Internet Freedom Foundation calls on SBI to inform every affected customer directly and without further delay.

We regret to note that the law in force today does not compel the bank to do so. Section 8(6) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires a Data Fiduciary to intimate a personal data breach to the Data Protection Board and to each affected Data Principal, and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules, 2025 prescribes how this is to be done. But the Union Government chose a staggered commencement, and these provisions will take effect only on 13 May 2027, nearly four years after Parliament enacted the law. The reporting obligations that apply today, under the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 and the RBI’s cyber security framework for banks, are owed to regulators and not to customers. A listed bank is bound to keep the stock exchanges informed. No law in force clearly binds it to inform the people whose data it holds.

Our demands

1. SBI must inform each affected customer by SMS, email and letter to the registered address, in English, Hindi and the language of the customer’s branch, stating what data was exposed and what steps they should take. It should open a dedicated helpline and an online facility for customers to check whether their data is affected.

2. SBI must state what the 3.75 lakh records and the 2,722 documents contain, how many customers they relate to, and whether they include KYC documents such as Aadhaar, PAN or passport copies.

3. When the investigation concludes, SBI must disclose how the data left its systems, including whether it came through a vendor or a direct selling agent, and publish a summary of the investigating agency’s findings.

4. The Reserve Bank of India should direct all regulated entities to notify customers of personal data breaches within a fixed period, pending the commencement of the DPDP Act.

5. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology should bring Section 8(6) of the DPDP Act and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules into force immediately.

On 22 September 2026, IFF filed RTI applications with MoRTH and NIC asking who has access to VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC data. NIC’s reply of 16 October discloses that 25,314 credentials were issued to private entities and that 17.08 million queries were run through them in 33 months. It also says private sharing was discontinued from 1 October 2026 on MoRTH’s directions, a decision we have found announced nowhere. (1/8)

Read More: https://t.co/ky7ppU9Hlc

The switch-off covers only private entities. Under clause 4.3 of the NTR Policy, police and law enforcement agencies keep complete access to every field, including personal data, with no consent or judicial check. In Delhi, this access underpins the Safe City camera network, the ANPR cameras at border points and e-Challan. It will also underpin the ₹1,789.52 crore Intelligent Traffic Management System approved on 30 September, which will be integrated with VAHAN. (7/8)

We filed a first appeal against MoRTH on 6 October and are appealing NIC’s reply. The first relief we seek is a direction to preserve the logs that remain. We are also seeking a copy of the discontinuation direction. Our further demands are a public register of everyone with access to NTR data, deletion of data already shared, longer log retention, notification to vehicle owners whose records were accessed, and a statutory basis for police access. (8/8) Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

MoRTH disposed of our application in two days and answered none of our twelve questions. Its reply said the Ministry deals with the Motor Vehicles Act, that implementation is for the States, and that a data sharing policy is available online. It cited no exemption and gave no appeal particulars, both of which Section 7(8) of the RTI Act requires. It was written on 24 September, a week before the switch-off, and does not mention it. The same Ministry disclosed recipient names and revenue figures to Parliament in 2019 and 2021. (5/8)

Ending private sharing is a welcome step, but it was done without a public order, a Gazette entry or a news report. An arrangement switched off without a stated reason can be switched back on the same way. We still don’t know why it was ended, whether recipients must delete the data they already hold, or whether this is permanent. Meanwhile, the ₹29 app is still live on the Play Store, with 10M+ downloads, as of 17 October. (6/8)
